questions.stem: A PharmD graduate from an approved Massachusetts pharmacy school has not yet received a pharmacist license. The graduate still holds a valid Massachusetts intern license and works under a registered pharmacist preceptor's direct supervision. The graduate is not enrolled in a residency. What is the correct licensure conclusion?

choices.text: Graduation immediately cancels every pharmacy intern's authority to practice, even while the intern license remains valid.
choices.why: Incorrect. Under 247 CMR 8.01(10), an approved-school graduate may continue acting as an intern until licensed as a pharmacist.

choices.text: The graduate may act as an independent pharmacist when the NAPLEX application has been accepted.
choices.why: Incorrect. Approval to seek examination is not a pharmacist license and does not remove direct intern supervision.

choices.text: The graduate may work only as a pharmacy technician trainee after graduation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 8.01(10) expressly continues intern authority; automatic downgrading to a trainee is not required.

choices.text: The graduate may continue as a pharmacy intern under the required supervision until becoming licensed as a pharmacist.
choices.why: Correct. The 8.01(10) graduate continuation is not limited to approved residency participants; 8.01(3) direct supervision still applies.

choices.text: Only an employer-issued affidavit, rather than a current Board intern license, is needed to act as a pharmacist.
choices.why: Incorrect. Graduation and employment documentation do not independently authorize a pharmacist's unsupervised duties.

questions.material_novelty: Tests ordinary approved PharmD graduate continuing an existing intern license without residency, unlike previous residency-specific eligibility.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the graduate becomes licensed as a pharmacist, the person may practice pursuant to that pharmacist license rather than an intern-only pathway.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy technician's most recent state license expiration was on the technician's birthday two years ago. The technician has maintained national certification but did not renew the Massachusetts technician license. A supervisor proposes waiting until December 31 to complete the state renewal. What is correct?

choices.text: The active national certification automatically extends the Massachusetts state technician license until the end of an even-numbered year.
choices.why: Incorrect. The technician license has a separate Massachusetts expiration and cannot be extended merely by national certification.

choices.text: Massachusetts technician licenses expire every two years on the licensee's birthdate, and practice after lapse is unlicensed practice.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.07(1)–(2) ties the technician's expiration to the birthdate and bars practice after expiration.

choices.text: All Massachusetts pharmacy personnel, including technicians, have the same December 31 pharmacist-license expiration.
choices.why: Incorrect. The pharmacist personal-registration renewal cycle is not the 247 CMR 8.07 technician rule.

choices.text: An unrenewed technician license remains valid until the pharmacy Manager of Record asks for a new copy.
choices.why: Incorrect. The state expiration is not contingent on a manager's request.

choices.text: A pharmacy technician's national certification permanently substitutes for any Board-issued technician license.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.04(1) still requires a valid Board technician license for certified technician work.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the state technician license's birthday-based biennial expiration, not loss of national certification or employment-start license verification.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the worker renews the Massachusetts technician license before expiration, the unlicensed-practice issue disappears.

questions.stem: The Board asks a Massachusetts retail pharmacy's Manager of Record to document how its pharmacy technician trainees, ordinary technicians, and certified technicians are used. The manager produces only the work schedule and says no written description of delegated duties exists. What must be available on request?

choices.text: Only the corporate labor budget; state pharmacy rules do not cover the content of delegated duties.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 8.06(1) expressly requires written information describing delegated duties and scopes.

choices.text: The pharmacy's current fill counts are sufficient, even if the manager cannot explain which jobs were delegated.
choices.why: Incorrect. Production counts do not substitute for required role-specific delegation documentation.

choices.text: Only documents concerning nationally certified technicians are required, not ordinary technicians or trainees.
choices.why: Incorrect. 8.06(1) explicitly includes all three categories.

choices.text: A signed annual statement that every technician may independently resolve drug interactions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Independent clinical conflict resolution is outside technician scope and a blanket authorization is not compliant documentation.

choices.text: An employee list and written descriptions of delegated tasks and scopes of responsibility for technicians and trainees.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.06(1)(a)–(c) identifies each requested category, including personnel list, delegated duties and responsibility scope.

questions.material_novelty: Tests documentation that Board can demand about role delegation, not numerical personnel ratios or which technician independently counsels.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the manager has current employee listings and written authorized delegation descriptions, the missing-record defect is resolved.

questions.stem: A pharmacist seeking renewal in Massachusetts received an out-of-state disciplinary sanction solely for dispensing medication for reproductive healthcare services that would have been lawful in Massachusetts and were consistent with good Massachusetts professional practice. No separate unsafe or fraudulent conduct is found. What does 247 CMR 8.08 provide?

choices.text: The out-of-state action automatically revokes the pharmacist's Massachusetts license before any review.
choices.why: Incorrect. The specific Massachusetts protection is intended to prevent denial for the stated legally protected healthcare activity alone.

choices.text: The pharmacist is exempt from all other Massachusetts renewal requirements for life.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision protects against denial on the specified ground; it does not waive unrelated renewal requirements.

choices.text: Renewal may not be denied solely because of the qualifying out-of-state sanction for legally protected healthcare activity.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 8.08 applies where the underlying service would be legal in Massachusetts and satisfies its good-practice standard.

choices.text: The rule allows a licensee to ignore Massachusetts professional practice standards whenever the service concerns reproductive healthcare.
choices.why: Incorrect. Conformity with Massachusetts good professional practice standards is an express condition.

choices.text: The renewal protection applies only if the applicant was never sanctioned or investigated outside Massachusetts.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision expressly discusses outside complaints, charges, judgments and discipline tied to covered activity.

questions.citation: 247 CMR 8.08; M.G.L. c.12 §11½ (definition of covered services)
questions.material_novelty: Tests a statutory carve-out for otherwise-lawful reproductive and gender-affirming care rather than general out-of-state discipline.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the sanction arose from objectively unsafe care also unlawful or below professional standards in Massachusetts, this specific exclusion would not automatically shield the conduct.

questions.stem: A chain pharmacy offers a prescriber free stacks of blank prescription forms prominently preprinted with the chain's store name and address so patients will bring future prescriptions there. No patient-specific prescription has yet been written. What does Massachusetts pharmacy law say?

choices.text: A pharmacy licensee may not provide a practitioner with blank prescription forms that refer to a pharmacist or pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.01(14) expressly prohibits licensees providing practitioners with pharmacy-referencing blank prescription forms.

choices.text: The preprinted forms are permitted if the pharmacy also offers a discount card.
choices.why: Incorrect. A discount does not waive the specific blank-form prohibition.

choices.text: Only blank forms naming a particular prescriber are restricted; pharmacy-branded blanks are always allowed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule addresses forms that refer to a pharmacist or pharmacy.

choices.text: The pharmacy may avoid the restriction by asking the prescriber's office staff to collect and distribute the blank forms.
choices.why: Incorrect. Indirect distribution does not turn pharmacy-supplied referral forms into compliant practice.

choices.text: Blank pharmacy-referencing prescription forms are permitted whenever the first fill is for a Schedule VI drug.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.01(14) is not confined to Schedule II–V prescribing.

questions.material_novelty: Tests pharmacy-sponsored blank prescription form distribution and steering rather than generic drug interchange or label contents.
questions.counterfactual_flip: A blank prescription form that does not refer to a particular pharmacist or pharmacy avoids this particular pharmacy-referencing prohibition, though other laws still apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy advertises 'every prescription dispensed by an on-site pharmacist' even though it routinely processes and releases some prescriptions while no pharmacist is present under a purported workaround. Assume the statement is materially false. Which legal ground directly addresses the advertisement?

choices.text: The statement becomes lawful merely because the pharmacy's website includes a disclaimer about business hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. A general-hours disclaimer does not cure a materially misleading representation about pharmacist service.

choices.text: Massachusetts permits inaccurate pharmacy advertising whenever a technician is nationally certified.
choices.why: Incorrect. Certification has no effect on the false or misleading advertising prohibition.

choices.text: The false statement is exempt from regulation because prescription records are confidential.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient confidentiality does not authorize inaccurate public advertising.

choices.text: 247 CMR 9.03 prohibits pharmacy licensees from engaging in false, deceptive, or misleading advertising.
choices.why: Correct. The regulation expressly prohibits this kind of public representation regardless of specific drug schedule.

choices.text: Only FDA, not the Massachusetts Board, may regulate statements made in pharmacy marketing.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Board's 247 CMR 9.03 independently applies to its pharmacy licensees.

questions.material_novelty: Tests independent Massachusetts advertising truthfulness rather than HIPAA disclosure permission or manufacturer product advertisements.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the claimed on-site pharmacist process is consistently true and other advertising requirements are met, the stated false-advertising violation disappears.

questions.stem: A customer urgently asks a Massachusetts pharmacy for a naloxone rescue kit. The pharmacy's last eligible kit was dispensed earlier today, and none can be supplied now. The pharmacy is also situated in an area that the Board has officially designated a high-overdose area. Which obligations follow 247 CMR 9.06? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A pharmacy in a designated high-overdose area must maintain a continuous supply of naloxone kits or other approved opioid antagonists readily available for dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.06(2)(a) imposes the continuous-supply duty in designated areas.

choices.text: The pharmacy's lack of stock ends its responsibilities; there is no referral duty for a customer requesting a kit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.06(4) requires referral when the kit is not readily available.

choices.text: The pharmacy must refer the requestor to the nearest location that currently has an approved opioid antagonist available.
choices.why: Correct. This is the specific response prescribed in 9.06(4).

choices.text: A pharmacy outside a high-overdose area is always prohibited from dispensing an opioid antagonist under a valid standing order.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.06(2)(b) allows dispensing outside such areas under a standing order or prescription.

choices.text: The supply and referral duties are subject to the patient's opioid's federal Schedule II classification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The statutory pharmacy naloxone availability pathway is not conditioned on which opioid the person may have taken.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the geographically triggered continuing stock requirement and the no-stock nearest-supplier referral duty, not naloxone standing-order permission.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy has kits readily available, the no-stock referral duty in 9.06(4) is not triggered.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy assembles a kit containing a labeled naloxone product and other appropriate rescue supplies and dispenses the finished rescue kit to an eligible requester. Which requirements are supported by 247 CMR 9.06? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The pharmacy may label the outer kit merely 'OTC supplies' without identifying it as an opioid antagonist rescue kit.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.06(5) specifies the required outer-kit identification.

choices.text: The dispensing pharmacy must provide counseling when supplying the opioid antagonist kit.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.06(3) requires counseling at the time of dispensing.

choices.text: The pharmacy must supply the Board-approved opioid antagonist information pamphlet with the rescue kit.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.06(3) identifies the accompanying pamphlet.

choices.text: The outer package must identify the kit as an opioid antagonist rescue kit, or by the particular antagonist's name followed by 'Rescue Kit'.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.06(5) expressly supplies the two approved outer label styles.

choices.text: The assembled kit must bear an expiration date based on the expiration date of the included drug unit.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.06(5) requires this expiration basis.

questions.material_novelty: Tests kit assembly, component-based expiry and mandated counseling/pamphlet, not pharmacist's authority to supply naloxone to a third-party requester.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy dispenses a sealed retail OTC naloxone package rather than assembling a kit, the custom kit-assembly outer-label rule is not triggered.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy does NOT hold a separate Drug Store Pharmacy license. An employed hospital pharmacist receives otherwise valid prescriptions for a hospital nurse, the nurse's spouse living with the nurse, an unrelated neighbor, and a hospital outpatient. Assume no other statutory permission applies. Who may ordinarily receive medications under the hospital-pharmacy exception?

choices.text: Only currently admitted inpatients; employees and outpatients are categorically excluded.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.01(13) expressly includes outpatients and employees as well as certain household family members.

choices.text: The nurse, spouse, unrelated neighbor and outpatient, because one employee can nominate additional local residents.
choices.why: Incorrect. A neighbor is not made eligible merely through knowing an employee.

choices.text: Any resident in the hospital's postal code if a hospital staff member enters the order.
choices.why: Incorrect. Geographic residence alone is not an authorized recipient category.

choices.text: The neighbor and nurse but not the nurse's spouse, because only workers and their friends are covered.
choices.why: Incorrect. The household spouse is included in the exception; the unrelated friend/neighbor is not.

choices.text: The hospital nurse, spouse living in the nurse's household, and hospital outpatient, but not the unrelated neighbor.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.01(13) permits hospital inpatients/outpatients, employees, and employees' co-resident spouses and children.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the hospital employee/co-resident spouse recipient exception rather than the already-tested hospital inpatient-versus-walk-in population limit.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the spouse lives separately from the employee, the regulation's co-residence requirement for this exception is absent.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacist works in an inpatient unit under a valid medication order. The unit's counsel sign-off procedure is being copied directly from a community pharmacy. Which statement correctly describes 247 CMR 9.18's scope?

choices.text: Its specific community patient-counseling provisions generally do not apply to pharmacists practicing in an inpatient setting unless another law or regulation requires otherwise.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.18(10) expressly states this practice-setting limitation.

choices.text: Hospital pharmacists must never counsel hospitalized patients about medications.
choices.why: Incorrect. The section's scope exception does not prohibit appropriate inpatient patient education or other duties.

choices.text: Every inpatient medication administration must follow the same retail pickup-sign requirement, irrespective of inpatient law.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation provides an inpatient scope carve-out; other applicable laws can still govern.

choices.text: The inpatient exception eliminates the hospital pharmacist's responsibility to assess the safety of patient drug therapy.
choices.why: Incorrect. Scope of this counseling section does not remove clinical or professional duties.

choices.text: All outpatient retail pharmacy counseling rules become inapplicable merely because the pharmacy belongs to a hospital corporation.
choices.why: Incorrect. The relevant condition is pharmacist practice in an inpatient setting, not corporate ownership.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the explicitly stated inpatient practice-setting exception rather than waiver of outpatient pickup counseling.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacist is instead dispensing to an ordinary outpatient under the retail procedure, the 9.18 inpatient exception is not established.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts drug store pharmacy proposes paying a nursing home's admissions coordinator $30 for each resident whose prescriptions are directed to that pharmacy. The coordinator is an employee of the nursing home. The payment is explicitly for generating pharmacy business, not for unrelated services. What follows from Massachusetts professional practice rules?

choices.text: This is allowed because nursing-home staff are not included in federal Medicare provider billing definitions.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.01(11) expressly covers remuneration to facility personnel for referrals regardless of this billing premise.

choices.text: The pharmacy may pay the coordinator as long as patients are also told they have a freedom of pharmacy choice.
choices.why: Incorrect. A general statement about choice does not waive the state referral-remuneration prohibition.

choices.text: The payment arrangement is prohibited by 247 CMR 9.01(11), which bars remuneration connected with health-care facility referrals or pharmacy business generation.
choices.why: Correct. Payments to nursing home employees for referrals fall within the specific stated prohibition.

choices.text: The pharmacy may substitute gift cards for cash without changing the legal result.
choices.why: Incorrect. The rule covers anything of value, not only cash; gift cards remain prohibited remuneration.

choices.text: The payment is permitted whenever the resident takes a noncontrolled Schedule VI drug.
choices.why: Incorrect. The prohibition is not conditional on the drug's schedule.

questions.material_novelty: Tests prohibited payment for nursing-home referrals rather than lawful workplace collection or discharge bedside delivery.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If no compensation or anything of value is connected to a referral or generation of business, this specific remuneration-based violation may not arise.

questions.stem: During a confirmed failure of the computerized label printer, a Massachusetts community pharmacy must prepare an urgent, otherwise legally valid outpatient prescription. The pharmacist can review the medication and produce a clearly legible handwritten label containing all required information. What does 247 CMR 9.04(3) allow?

choices.text: All prescription dispensing must stop until the printer works, even when the legal emergency alternative is available.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation includes an express temporary label-making exception for a printing or equipment failure.

choices.text: A legibly handwritten or typed prescription label may be used during the emergency period.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.04(3) expressly provides for legible handwritten or typed labeling when printing/equipment fails.

choices.text: The pharmacy may omit patient identifiers from handwritten labels because the drug is urgently needed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The emergency permits the labeling method to change, not required label content to disappear.

choices.text: The pharmacy may use no label and instead give the patient verbal drug instructions.
choices.why: Incorrect. It still must label the prescription in conformity with the substantive legal requirements.

choices.text: An assistant may release a new unchecked prescription because the label printer is down.
choices.why: Incorrect. This exception does not waive pharmacist final validation or DUR.

questions.material_novelty: Tests the expressly allowed emergency handwritten-label exception, not general electronic downtime profile recovery or patient label elements.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If there is no printer/equipment failure or emergency period, routine labels must be printed clearly by the computerized system.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist dispenses an otherwise lawful prescription for a drug distributed solely under its GENERIC name. The product does NOT have an NDC number. The manufacturer's name is available from the supplied stock information. What must the pharmacy record under 247 CMR 9.04(7)?

choices.text: Nothing, because a generic-name-only product is exempt from all medication-identification records.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.04(7) expressly calls for a substitute identification when no NDC exists.

choices.text: Only the patient's insurance billing identifier.
choices.why: Incorrect. Insurance billing does not replace the specified manufacturer identification.

choices.text: Any prescriber's DEA number, even if the product is a Schedule VI drug and the number is irrelevant.
choices.why: Incorrect. The section concerns the distributed product's identifying source, not a substitute DEA number.

choices.text: Record the manufacturer's name in the computerized system; if that name is unavailable, record the distributor, packer or repacker.
choices.why: Correct. This is the exact hierarchy in 247 CMR 9.04(7) when a generic-only product has no NDC.

choices.text: Ask the prescriber to issue a replacement prescription containing a fictional NDC.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation supplies an alternative manufacturer identification; inventing an NDC is inappropriate.

questions.material_novelty: Contrasts optional NDC in the prescriber's controlled Rx (D033) with separate manufacturer-data entry when a generic-only dispensed product has no NDC.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the distributed generic drug has a valid NDC, record that NDC instead of invoking the no-NDC manufacturer fallback.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts patient asks Pharmacy B to refill a reusable daily dosage planner using tablets that Pharmacy A already dispensed to the patient last week. Pharmacy B is capable of cleaning and labeling the planner and can verify the original drug bottle. What is the correct decision under 247 CMR 9.07?

choices.text: Refill the planner using Pharmacy A's previously dispensed tablets after the patient signs a waiver.
choices.why: Incorrect. The prohibition on medications previously dispensed by another pharmacy is not waived by patient consent.

choices.text: Refill it if Pharmacy A emails the receipt, because an accurate invoice makes the tablets transferable stock.
choices.why: Incorrect. The source restriction is based on prior dispensing by another pharmacy, not proof of purchase.

choices.text: Refill it with the previously dispensed medication if the drug is only Schedule VI.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.07(1) does not restrict the prohibition to federally controlled drugs.

choices.text: Treat a reusable planner as exempt from 247 CMR 9.07 when it has seven or fewer compartments.
choices.why: Incorrect. There is no small-compartment exception in the section.

choices.text: Do not place Pharmacy A's previously dispensed medication into Pharmacy B's reusable dosage planner; use a legally compliant alternative.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.07(1) prohibits inclusion of drugs previously dispensed by a different pharmacy.

questions.material_novelty: Tests a reusable *daily dosage planner* supplied from a second pharmacy's already-dispensed pills, not multi-drug unit-dose packaging returned to the original dispensing pharmacy.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If Pharmacy B instead dispenses qualifying medications from its own lawful stock and follows the planner-labeling rules, the interpharmacy prior-dispensing prohibition would not apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy wants to make ORAL-LIQUID-SINGLE-DOSE packets. For Patient A, it plans to combine two different commercially available liquid medications in one packet without compounding under a patient-specific prescription. For Patient B, the physician issued a valid compounded-preparation order, and the pharmacy can meet the appropriate compounding and labeling requirements. Which conclusions are supported by 247 CMR 9.08? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Combining the two commercial liquid medicines for Patient A is prohibited under the ordinary oral-liquid-single-dose rule.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.08(1)(h) bars placing more than one commercially available medicine into a liquid single-dose package absent lawful prescription compounding.

choices.text: Patient A's combined packet automatically becomes lawful if a technician signs the final label.
choices.why: Incorrect. Technician signature does not overcome the subsection's compounding-prescription condition or pharmacist responsibility.

choices.text: The rule bars every oral-liquid-single-dose package, even when it contains just one appropriate medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.08(1) expressly recognizes oral-liquid-single-dose packaging when applicable requirements are met.

choices.text: A lawfully compounded prescription for Patient B may qualify for the stated exception, subject to all applicable compounding safeguards.
choices.why: Correct. The 'unless compounded pursuant to a prescription' text permits this distinct route with otherwise required conditions.

choices.text: The individual package must still meet applicable packaging compatibility and patient-labeling requirements.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.08(1)(c)–(g) and (5) continue to govern compliant packaging and labeling.

questions.material_novelty: Tests single-dose liquid multi-product packaging's explicit compounding-prescription exception, distinct from earlier solid multi-drug packs and USP nonsterile compounding limits.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If Patient A uses a single qualifying commercial liquid per package, or the two liquids are lawfully compounded pursuant to a prescription, the specific two-commercial-medicine prohibition may not apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy lawfully substitutes a LESS EXPENSIVE BRAND-NAME drug product for the originally prescribed brand, using an authorized interchangeable product. All other label elements are met. Under 247 CMR 9.05(3)(b), which interchange-label content is allowed?

choices.text: No 'interchange' designation because the substituted product is another brand rather than a generic.
choices.why: Incorrect. Subsection (3)(b) specifically addresses a less-expensive brand product interchange.

choices.text: Only the originally prescribed brand, concealing the different product actually dispensed.
choices.why: Incorrect. The interchange labeling must identify the dispensed lower-priced product in one of the permitted ways.

choices.text: The 'interchange' designation followed by either the dispensed lower-priced brand name or its generic name and manufacturer.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.05(3)(b) expressly permits either labeled form for a substituted lower-cost brand product.

choices.text: Only a manufacturer's NDC; Massachusetts rules prohibit naming a product dispensed through interchange.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation directs product-name-based interchange notation, not NDC-only disclosure.

choices.text: The patient may choose any label description, even if it does not accurately identify the substituted medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient preference does not waive the legally required identification of dispensed interchange product.

questions.material_novelty: Tests interchangeable cheaper *brand-name* labeling, distinct from previous generic-product interchange labeling and underlying eligibility.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If an ordinary cheaper generic is dispensed instead, 9.05(3)(a)'s generic name/manufacturer label format governs.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy purchases a comprehensive human-drug database and concludes it no longer needs any current veterinary reference or updated Massachusetts interchangeable-drug references. Its Manager of Record wants to satisfy 247 CMR 9.19(1). Which statements describe required information access? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Only a current federal DEA schedule list is required; Massachusetts interchange references are optional.
choices.why: Incorrect. The Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs and the specific included lists are required.

choices.text: The pharmacy must maintain a current Massachusetts List of Interchangeable Drugs, including the Orange Book and applicable lists.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(1)(a) enumerates this specific source.

choices.text: The pharmacy is exempt from a veterinary reference because the pharmacy fills very few animal prescriptions.
choices.why: Incorrect. 9.19(1)(d) does not create that volume-based exemption for ordinary resident Drug Store Pharmacies.

choices.text: The pharmacy must retain current laws and regulations or readily available electronic access to them for pharmacy practice.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(1)(c) lists legal materials and permits electronic access.

choices.text: Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook or another Board-approved veterinary reference must be available in current or electronic form.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(1)(d) expressly requires an acceptable veterinary reference.

questions.material_novelty: Tests required professional reference resources at pharmacy premises rather than whether a veterinarian can write a Schedule VI prescription.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy is an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy, 9.19(24) creates exemptions from certain specific reference requirements, including 9.19(1)(a) and (d).

questions.topic: Schedule II inventory entries versus corrections
questions.stem: A Massachusetts resident pharmacy identifies a discrepancy in its perpetual Schedule II inventory. A certified pharmacy technician made an ordinary documented receipt entry earlier that morning. The pharmacist Manager of Record is off site, but a pharmacist has been appointed as the Manager of Record's designee. Which statements are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A certified pharmacy technician may make ordinary entries in the Schedule II perpetual inventory under applicable supervision and security policies.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(f) permits certified pharmacy technician entries.

choices.text: A certified technician may independently adjust the perpetual inventory to erase a discrepancy if the technician originally entered the purchase.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.21(8)(d) assigns discrepancy-related adjustments to the Manager of Record or pharmacist designee in the Manager's absence.

choices.text: The Manager of Record normally must investigate an inventory discrepancy and determine whether any significant loss or suspected theft reporting is necessary.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.21(8)(c) assigns discrepancy investigation and applicable reports to the Manager of Record.

choices.text: In the Manager of Record's absence, a pharmacist designee may make an adjustment and report the change to the Manager of Record.
choices.why: Correct. This is the specific exception in 9.21(8)(d).

choices.text: An unlicensed cashier may perform an inventory adjustment when the pharmacist later cosigns the printout.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.21(8)(e) says an unlicensed individual may not make an entry or adjust the perpetual inventory.

questions.material_novelty: Separates certified-technician *data entry* from pharmacist/MOR *adjustment authority* and the pharmacist-designee absence exception, not the earlier ten-day inventory reconciliation test.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the manager is present, the pharmacist-designee-in-absence adjustment exception would not apply without other authority.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy operates inside a grocery store. The grocery store is open 8 a.m.–10 p.m., but the pharmacy is open 9 a.m.–6 p.m. Management plans to print a promotional flyer listing only the grocery-store hours and place the pharmacy's true hours on a small sign behind the pharmacy counter. What correction is required by 247 CMR 9.19(14)?

choices.text: Only the flyer should change; posting hours at the grocery store's consumer entrances is never required.
choices.why: Incorrect. 9.19(14)(a) independently requires pharmacy-hour postings at consumer entrances and the pharmacy.

choices.text: The pharmacy must keep the same hours as the grocery store or surrender its pharmacy license.
choices.why: Incorrect. Different hours are contemplated; accurate posting and pharmacy-advertising disclosure are required.

choices.text: The flyer need not mention pharmacy hours because it is the supermarket that owns the building.
choices.why: Incorrect. When an advertisement refers to the pharmacy and the hours differ, the pharmacy hours must be clearly specified.

choices.text: The store may show retail hours alone if a cashier verbally tells customers the pharmacy's shorter hours on request.
choices.why: Incorrect. Oral explanations do not replace required postings and clear advertising.

choices.text: Post pharmacy hours at all applicable consumer entrances and at the pharmacy, and clearly specify pharmacy hours in advertisements referring to the pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. Both requirements appear in 247 CMR 9.19(14)(a)–(b).

questions.material_novelty: Tests distinct public posting and advertising obligations for a pharmacy inside a longer-hours retail establishment, not pharmacy alarms at closure.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the supermarket and pharmacy have identical hours, the different-hours advertisement requirement in 9.19(14)(b) is not triggered, though 9.19(14)(a) postings still apply.

questions.stem: A Massachusetts resident retail pharmacy is reviewing a Board inspection checklist. The pharmacy has a current state Drug Store Pharmacy license, Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration (MCSR), and DEA registration, but management stores each only in a locked corporate office and shows none in the public pharmacy. Which statements apply under 247 CMR 9.19(8)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The resident pharmacy may satisfy its display obligation by keeping all credentials only at an out-of-state corporate headquarters.
choices.why: Incorrect. Resident Massachusetts pharmacies must conspicuously display the enumerated documents within the pharmacy.

choices.text: The Massachusetts Drug Store Pharmacy license must be conspicuously displayed within the resident pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.19(8)(a) specifically lists this facility license.

choices.text: The pharmacy's MCSR and DEA registrations must also be conspicuously displayed within the resident pharmacy.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 9.19(8)(c)–(d) identify both.

choices.text: Every nonresident pharmacy shipping into Massachusetts must display these documents on a Massachusetts facility wall, even if it has no physical site there.
choices.why: Incorrect. For nonresident pharmacies the regulation instead calls for documents kept readily retrievable.

choices.text: A nonresident pharmacy may keep the listed credentials readily retrievable rather than conspicuously displayed within a Massachusetts premises.
choices.why: Correct. The final sentence of 9.19(8) expressly distinguishes nonresident status.

questions.material_novelty: Tests resident *facility* credential display versus nonresident document retrievability, different from pharmacist personal-license availability.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy is a nonresident rather than a Massachusetts-located Drug Store Pharmacy, the regulation's readily retrievable document rule applies.
